palette: powder blue tile against white and chrome
topic: brushing one wall and leaving the rest of the photo untouched
angle: Masking Studio changes the region you paint and nothing else. Everything outside the brush is the original photograph rather than a re-render that happens to look similar, which is the claim a whole-photo tool cannot make.
visualSummary: A single deep blue frame holding one photo card of a bathroom, split down the middle by a vertical seam with a drag handle, BEFORE pill on the left and AFTER pill on the right. The room is a white freestanding bath against a large square tiled wall, a chrome floor standing tap rising beside it, two rolled grey towels on the rim, a window throwing daylight from the left. Left of the seam the wall is plain off white ceramic; right of it the same wall is powder blue on the same tile grid. Because both halves are the same photograph, the bath, the tap, the towels and the window run unbroken across the seam and only the tile changes colour. A capsule of copy sits under the card. Powder blue and white against the blue chrome.

copy.headline: One wall. Nothing else.
copy.caption:
We brushed one wall. The bath, the tap and the towels are the same pixels they were before.

That is the whole of Masking Studio. You paint over the part you want changed, and everything outside the brush is left exactly as it was. Not re-rendered, not redrawn. The original file.

The alternative is restaging the whole photo, and that gives you a new room rather than a new wall. The bath moves. The tap grows a second handle. The light from the window lands somewhere else. It all looks fine until you put it next to the picture you started with.

So here is the check. Run your eye across the seam. The bath rim carries straight through it without a step, and the grout lines meet on both sides. Only the tile changes colour.

We measured it rather than trusting it: of the 118,054 pixels outside the brushed area, zero changed.

One photo. One brush. One pass.

Save this for the next time a client asks what a different tile would look like.

Virtually staged with Stagify.ai

license.prompt: Photorealistic interior photograph of a finished, furnished bathroom, shot in portrait orientation from across the room, wide enough to read as a whole room. One large flat wall of plain square ceramic tile facing the camera, filling much of the frame, clear of mirrors and cabinets. Soft even daylight, no people, no toilet. A white freestanding bath sits low against the tiled wall, with a chrome floor standing tap beside it and a folded towel on a rail. A window to one side.

images.altText: A white freestanding bath against a large white tiled wall, with a chrome tap.
images.note: Generated rather than stock, and not for want of trying: thirty photographs across ten stock queries were screened and every one rejected, because a real bathroom almost always has a mirror, a vanity or a glass screen crossing its main tiled wall. This post needed one broad uninterrupted wall, since the model retiles a large area cleanly and declines to retile a narrow strip. The uncropped room is archived in the source store under sourceSha256; the before frame here is that room downscaled by the route and cropped by the SAME rectangle as the after frame.

images.altText: The same bathroom with the tiled wall retiled in powder blue.

generation.fn: brush mask composited over the pipeline source
generation.note:
The recoloured wall was rendered in Stagify by the account owner and supplied as a finished image, rather than coming from this tool's own mask-edit run. Confirmed product output, so the post advertises Stagify with Stagify's work.

It arrived as a full-frame render: 94.5 per cent of the pixels OUTSIDE the wall differed from the source, worst pixel 721 of 765, and the tap had been redrawn to a different shape. Shipped as delivered it would have made three of the four legend rows false, since they each promise 'the same pixels'. So the supplied wall was composited over the pipeline's own source through the same brush mask: the tile inside the brush is the supplied render, everything outside it is the original photograph, and the delivered frames now differ in exactly one place. The supplied grout grid aligned with the source geometry, so the join carries no seam.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: It is the only shortlisted candidate whose payoff is not resolved on screen. The dorm grid, the tile grid and the plan-to-render all complete at the moment of looking; this one shows a claim you can only check by pointing the tool at your own room, so it earns an open rather than a like. It also answers the objection that actually stops this audience trying AI interiors at all, which is that the tool quietly redecorates things you did not ask about.
devilsAdvocate.whyNotTheOtherFour: i01 and i03 are both one room shown as N variants, the shape of the spare-room deck already in the queue, and both resolve fully on screen. i04 is a near reprint of the 07-30 plan-to-render post. i06 makes a claim about a typed prompt that the frame cannot show without fabricating interface chrome.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The proof is asserted, not shown. With no before frame the headline rests on the caption, and the mask boundary is exactly the geometry that comes back subtly wrong.
devilsAdvocate.howTheRiskLanded: It landed, repeatedly, and drove the whole build. The answer was to stop asserting and start measuring: the delivered frames are diffed pixel by pixel outside the brush, and the before frame was put on the slide beside the after so the viewer can check the claim rather than take it. The final layout is a seam rather than the pins the advocate's brief implied, because the pins tested as confusing.
